title: Southeast Asia's build-out strains power and capital
lede: Southeast Asia's data centre construction cycle accelerated through the week, with Malaysia's task force reporting more than 40 applications in 2026 and data centres accounting for 44 per cent of total investment into the country in the first half. Leasing momentum in Johor continued as Bitdeer AI committed to a second 65MW building, while the Philippines finalised a US$34.4 billion national AI infrastructure masterplan and Vietnam drew a new proposed development in Hai Phong. Australia advanced on multiple fronts: regulators approved Amazon's AUD 2.17 billion Sydney campus, Anthropic signed its first Australian lease, and OpenAI confirmed talks to train models locally. Yet the boom's strains are increasingly visible. Thailand forecast a nine-year high in power demand growth, YTL Power reserved additional gas turbines, and debt markets absorbed record-scale funding rounds from SoftBank, AirTrunk and others. Meanwhile, Huawei's Ascend roadmap and China's 82 new compute centre projects underscored the intensifying race for AI silicon and sovereign compute capacity across the region.

themes.heading: Malaysia's build-out deepens and localises
themes.narrative: Malaysia's Data Centre Task Force has assessed more than 40 proposals this year, and data centres accounted for 44 per cent of total investment into the country in 1H2026. Leasing activity in Johor remained strong, with Bitdeer AI taking a second 65MW building at the same campus under a 10-year agreement. Attention is now shifting to the local value chain: policymakers and industry experts argue the boom must produce domestic capabilities in semiconductors, cooling and power engineering, with contractors such as West River and Jati Tinggi already reorienting toward data centre work.

themes.heading: Australia and neighbours add capacity
themes.narrative: Australia moved forward on several fronts, with planning approval for Amazon's three-building, 235MW campus in western Sydney and Anthropic signing its first Australian lease at a Queensland digital park. OpenAI confirmed it is in talks to train models in Australia, while Nvidia expanded local AI infrastructure with partners. Elsewhere in the region, the Philippines finalised its US$34.4 billion AI infrastructure masterplan for 2026-2033 and BTC Digital signed an MOU to explore an AI data centre in Hai Phong, Vietnam.

themes.heading: Chip supply race intensifies across Asia
themes.narrative: Huawei positioned its Ascend 960 roadmap and an 11-chip portfolio as China's strongest answer to Nvidia, with rotating chairman Eric Xu saying domestic demand already exceeds production capacity. China's buildout continued at pace, with 82 new compute centre projects worth 181.7 billion yuan tallied in August alone. Supply-side manoeuvring extended beyond China: SK Hynix held talks with Intel on US memory production, Micron's Taiwan union pressed profit-sharing demands amid tight supply, and Nvidia partner GMI Cloud sought a US$300 million loan to buy chips for its Thai facility.

themes.heading: AI demand strains regional power systems
themes.narrative: Energy emerged as the binding constraint on the region's buildout. Thailand forecast power demand growth at a nine-year high on AI-driven investment, while YTL Power reserved four more Siemens gas turbines on top of three earlier units to serve regional demand. Developers are responding with supply-side innovation: Keppel plans to link an Indonesian solar project to Jurong Island and court data centre customers, a Johor facility made water management a core design priority, and AirTrunk partnered with Emergence Quantum on cryogenic cooling. Grid coordination also entered the agenda, with Nvidia, Google and Emerald AI launching an alliance for demand-responsive data centre power consumption.

themes.heading: Debt markets fund the AI build-out
themes.narrative: The week's financing activity underscored how deeply AI infrastructure now depends on global debt markets. SoftBank assembled nearly US$21 billion in new borrowings on top of an upsized US$11.9 billion loan for its OpenAI commitments, while SB Energy moved toward a US IPO with a Japanese tranche. AirTrunk sought roughly S$2 billion ahead of a potential Singapore listing, and S&P warned Malaysian operators may tap offshore dollar bonds as local banks tighten lending. Hong Kong illustrated the two-sided picture: developers face a US$2.6 billion funding gap as North American investors retreat, even as Goodman raised $455 million for a new facility, and Australian AI infrastructure firm Firmus opened its books to institutional investors while its founders mapped a path to realise billion-dollar stakes.

themes.heading: Debate grows over AI economics
themes.narrative: Sceptical voices grew louder this week. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's call to slow AI capability improvements triggered a selloff in Asian semiconductor stocks, reviving questions about the sustainability of infrastructure spending. Economists warned the data centre boom could pressure interest rates and housing by absorbing capital and construction resources, while a Goldman Sachs report found AI demand outpacing infrastructure and accelerating the shift to islanded, self-powered facilities. Industry figures pushed back: Nvidia's Jensen Huang argued no new AI laws are needed, and operators continue converting older industrial sites to capture existing grid connections.
